items: Assuming the branch is untouched while a range pick is stopped. Root cause: unlike a rebase, a cherry-pick commits on the branch as it goes; finished picks are already on it and HEAD is attached.
Using --quit to get out of a stopped pick. Root cause: it removes only the bookkeeping; the completed copies stay and the conflict stays in the index.
Resolving a pick conflict by taking "theirs" whole. Root cause: theirs is the full file from the other line, which may carry unrelated changes that the picked commit's parent already had.
Finishing a pick with git commit -m. Root cause: -m replaces the prepared message, including the line that -x wrote.

It runs in CI, the team's automation, at two in the morning. The second fix conflicts. The script doesn't check the exit status. It goes on to tag and build.

beats.text: Welcome back to Git and GitHub Deep Mastery. Pull up a chair. In the last video every cherry-pick finished in one step. Today they stop.
beats.tele: Welcome back to Git and GitHub Deep Mastery. Pull up a chair. In the last video every cherry-pick finished in one step. Today they stop.

beats.text: A cherry-pick can stop for two reasons. A conflict, where Git can't decide a file's content and waits for you. Or an empty result, because the change is already on your branch.

beats.text: The state. In one sentence: a stopped cherry-pick is described by one root ref, CHERRY_PICK_HEAD, and, when more than one commit was requested, by a directory .git/sequencer/ that holds the rest of the plan. A root ref is a name in capital letters that lives directly in the dot git folder.
beats.tele: The state. In one sentence: a stopped cherry-pick is described by one root ref, `CHERRY_PICK_HEAD`, and, when more than one commit was requested, by a directory `.git/sequencer/` that holds the rest of the plan. A root ref is a name in capital letters that lives directly in the dot git folder.

beats.text: CHERRY_PICK_HEAD is the commit that could not be applied. On screen it sits on ebcee16, on main. In .git/sequencer/, the file todo holds that commit and everything after it, and head is where HEAD was before the first pick. A cherry-pick of a single commit creates no sequencer directory at all. CHERRY_PICK_HEAD and the prepared message are its whole state.
beats.tele: `CHERRY_PICK_HEAD` is the commit that could not be applied. On screen it sits on `ebcee16`, on `main`. In `.git/sequencer/`, the file `todo` holds that commit and everything after it, and `head` is where HEAD was before the first pick. A cherry-pick of a single commit creates no sequencer directory at all. `CHERRY_PICK_HEAD` and the prepared message are its whole state.

beats.text: Now the difference from a rebase. HEAD is not detached. The picks that have already succeeded are on the branch. The branch has moved. Look at release/1.4: one copy, e0c8403, is already on it.
beats.tele: Now the difference from a rebase. HEAD is not detached. The picks that have already succeeded are on the branch. The branch has moved. Look at `release/1.4`: one copy, `e0c8403`, is already on it.

beats.text: Think about why. A rebase builds a replacement history off to the side and switches the branch over at the end. A cherry-pick adds commits to the branch you are on, one at a time. There is no "at the end".
beats.tele: Think about why. A rebase builds a replacement history off to the side and switches the branch over at the end. A cherry-pick adds commits to the branch you are on, one at a time. There is no "at the end".

beats.text: The four exits.
beats.tele: The four exits.

beats.text: The textbook labels --skip, --abort and --quit 🟡 CAUTION. --abort goes back to sequencer/head, so picks that had succeeded are undone as well, and resolution work is lost.
beats.tele: The textbook labels `--skip`, `--abort` and `--quit` 🟡 CAUTION. `--abort` goes back to `sequencer/head`, so picks that had succeeded are undone as well, and resolution work is lost.

beats.text: Conflicts. In one sentence: in a cherry-pick conflict, "ours" is your branch, "theirs" is the picked commit, and the base is the picked commit's parent: a version of the file that your branch may never have contained.
beats.tele: Conflicts. In one sentence: in a cherry-pick conflict, "ours" is your branch, "theirs" is the picked commit, and the base is the picked commit's parent: a version of the file that your branch may never have contained.

beats.text: Two things in that sentence. First, the sides are not swapped here as they are in a rebase: HEAD is your branch. Second, the base. It's not the merge base of the two branches. It's the parent of the picked commit, and that parent may already contain changes from its own branch that you have never had. On screen the base is 08f4771. The merge base, the most recent commit both branches share, is 93787ec.
beats.tele: Two things in that sentence. First, the sides are not swapped here as they are in a rebase: HEAD is your branch. Second, the base. It's not the merge base of the two branches. It's the parent of the picked commit, and that parent may already contain changes from its own branch that you have never had. On screen the base is `08f4771`. The merge base, the most recent commit both branches share, is `93787ec`.

beats.text: With the base in view, a conflict reads as an instruction: the change to carry over is the difference between base and theirs. Apply that difference to your version.
beats.tele: With the base in view, a conflict reads as an instruction: the change to carry over is the difference between base and theirs. Apply that difference to your version.

beats.text: Empty picks. In one sentence: when the picked change is already present on your branch, the merge result equals HEAD, there is nothing to commit, and --empty decides what happens next.
beats.tele: Empty picks. In one sentence: when the picked change is already present on your branch, the merge result equals HEAD, there is nothing to commit, and `--empty` decides what happens next.

beats.text: The textbook's version note. Older behavior: the only control was --keep-redundant-commits. Current behavior, since Git 2.45: --empty=(drop|keep|stop). Recommended: --empty=drop in scripts that backport lists of commits, so that a commit which is already present doesn't halt an unattended job.
beats.tele: The textbook's version note. Older behavior: the only control was `--keep-redundant-commits`. Current behavior, since Git 2.45: `--empty=(drop|keep|stop)`. Recommended: `--empty=drop` in scripts that backport lists of commits, so that a commit which is already present doesn't halt an unattended job.

beats.text: Picture two ways of laying a new stretch of track.
beats.tele: Picture two ways of laying a new stretch of track.

beats.text: A rebase lays the whole new stretch next to the old line, and when the last sleeper is down, it throws one switch. Until then trains still run on the old line. If work stops halfway, the old line is untouched.
beats.tele: A rebase lays the whole new stretch next to the old line, and when the last sleeper is down, it throws one switch. Until then trains still run on the old line. If work stops halfway, the old line is untouched.

beats.text: A cherry-pick of a range extends the line you are standing on, sleeper by sleeper. If work stops halfway, the line is longer than it was, and a train can already run onto the new part.
beats.tele: A cherry-pick of a range extends the line you are standing on, sleeper by sleeper. If work stops halfway, the line is longer than it was, and a train can already run onto the new part.

beats.text: Where does the picture break? The half-built rebase track is hard to find, since only a detached HEAD reaches it, while the half-extended cherry-pick line is in plain sight on the branch. That makes the cherry-pick state easier to see, and easier to ship by accident. A tag, a build or a push at that moment takes the partial result. Twig looks worried, and fairly so.

beats.text: --quit only deletes the bookkeeping. The completed copy stays on the branch, and the conflict stays in the index and the working tree: UU. And --continue afterwards says "no cherry-pick or revert in progress". This is the state the two-in-the-morning script would leave if it had tried to tidy up with the wrong exit.

beats.text: Author Asha Rao, committer Lab User, and the "cherry picked from commit" line in the message. The diff of the copy changes one thing, the argument, as the original did. That shortcut is tempting, and almost everyone tries it once.

beats.text: Five mistakes to watch for.
beats.tele: Five mistakes to watch for.

beats.text: Assuming the branch is untouched while a range pick is stopped. Root cause: unlike a rebase, a cherry-pick commits on the branch as it goes; finished picks are already on it and HEAD is attached.
beats.tele: Assuming the branch is untouched while a range pick is stopped. Root cause: unlike a rebase, a cherry-pick commits on the branch as it goes; finished picks are already on it and HEAD is attached.

beats.text: Using --quit to get out of a stopped pick. Root cause: it removes only the bookkeeping; the completed copies stay and the conflict stays in the index.
beats.tele: Using `--quit` to get out of a stopped pick. Root cause: it removes only the bookkeeping; the completed copies stay and the conflict stays in the index.

beats.text: Resolving a pick conflict by taking "theirs" whole. Root cause: theirs is the full file from the other line, which may carry unrelated changes that the picked commit's parent already had.
beats.tele: Resolving a pick conflict by taking "theirs" whole. Root cause: theirs is the full file from the other line, which may carry unrelated changes that the picked commit's parent already had.

beats.text: Finishing a pick with git commit -m. Root cause: -m replaces the prepared message, including the line that -x wrote.
beats.tele: Finishing a pick with `git commit -m`. Root cause: `-m` replaces the prepared message, including the line that `-x` wrote.

beats.text: Scripts that cherry-pick lists of commits without checking the exit status. Root cause: a conflict or an empty pick stops the sequence with a non-zero status and a partly advanced branch.
beats.tele: Scripts that cherry-pick lists of commits without checking the exit status. Root cause: a conflict or an empty pick stops the sequence with a non-zero status and a partly advanced branch.

beats.text: Now, out of the lab, and back to the script from the opening. The textbook's guidance is two sentences: a sequence that stops in a CI job or a release script leaves a branch that is partly advanced. A script that cherry-picks must check the exit status and decide: --abort to return to a known state, never a blind retry.
beats.tele: Now, out of the lab, and back to the script from the opening. The textbook's guidance is two sentences: a sequence that stops in a CI job or a release script leaves a branch that is partly advanced. A script that cherry-picks must check the exit status and decide: `--abort` to return to a known state, never a blind retry.

beats.text: For the release tooling of a model-serving team, that becomes three lines of policy. One: every git cherry-pick in a script is followed by a check of its exit status. Two: on failure the script runs git cherry-pick --abort and stops, and a person takes over with git status, which names the commit it was stuck on. Three: lists of backports are run with --empty=drop, so that a fix that is already present does not halt an unattended job.
beats.tele: For the release tooling of a model-serving team, that becomes three lines of policy. One: every `git cherry-pick` in a script is followed by a check of its exit status. Three: lists of backports are run with `--empty=drop`, so that a fix that is already present does not halt an unattended job.

beats.text: Answer out loud first. A strong answer is a comparison in parallel: for each of the two, where HEAD is, where the branch ref is, which ref names the commit being applied, and where the rest of the plan is stored. It then explains the difference from what each operation is building, so that it's a consequence and not a fact to memorize.
